Class Row

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.api.layout.Row
public final class Row extends Object
Lays elements out left to right: it positions each child with even spacing and a vertical alignment, and returns a flat list of positioned PanelElements.

A Row only exists while you build it. Don't keep it around to lay out again; add the returned elements to a Panel like any others.

Measured on first use. The positions are computed once, on the first read of any emitted element's position (in practice the panel's first layout pass), not in build(): a label's or button's size needs the game's font, which does not exist yet at mod init, where panels and dialogs are declared. So a Row builds anywhere. A Row holding a custom ElementSpec, whose element exists only once placed, is laid out in build() instead, measuring then.

Helper, not container. Row is not a PanelElement, does not render, and is gone once built. The Panel draws the elements directly, so a Panel stays the only thing that contains elements.

Usage

List<PanelElement> buttonRow = Row.at(20, 30).spacing(4)
    .add(Button.builder().label(Component.literal("OK")).size(60, 20).onClick(this::onConfirm).build())
    .add(Button.builder().label(Component.literal("Cancel")).size(60, 20).onClick(this::onCancel).build())
    .build();

Panel p = Panel.builder("confirm")
    .elements(buttonRow).style(PanelStyle.RAISED).build();

Pushing an element to the far edge

Row.Builder.width(int) declares the row's overall pixel width, and Row.Builder.addSpacer() adds a flexible gap that expands to fill whatever the other children and spacing leave over (like CSS justify-content: space-between), for a header with one thing on the left and another on the right: 
List<PanelElement> header = Row.at(0, 0).width(220).spacing(6)
    .add(Button.builder().label(Component.literal("Back")).size(60, 16).onClick(this::onBack).build())
    .addSpacer()
    .add(Button.builder().label(Component.literal("Reset")).size(60, 16).onClick(this::onReset).build())
    .build();
Several spacers in one row split the leftover evenly (the odd pixel to the last one), so a three-part header (one thing at each edge and one centred) is just two spacers.

Nesting

Rows and columns nest through Row.Builder.addRow(Consumer) and Row.Builder.addColumn(Consumer). Each lays its elements out from its own origin and the outer one offsets them, so build() still returns one flat list of positioned elements.
